title: Trump: White House prepares Alex Jones to lead Capitol march on January 6
description_short: Trump: White House prepares Alex Jones to lead Capitol march on January 6
description_medium: Before January 6, Alex Jones said someone from the White House asked him to lead a march to the Capitol and that Roger Stone had initially been considered. CNN separately reported that Jones helped organize the “Stop the Steal” rally. That reporting does not identify a White House caller or confirm the alleged request.
description_long: In the days before January 6, 2021, Alex Jones said someone from the White House asked him to lead a march to the Capitol and that Roger Stone had initially been considered. That alleged contact remains Jones’s account. CNN separately reported that Jones helped organize the “Stop the Steal” rally. Permit organizer Cindy Chafian told CNN that Jones contacted her to ensure he could speak and agreed to pay part of the event’s costs. CNN, citing the Wall Street Journal, reported that Publix heiress Julie Jenkins Fancelli contributed $300,000 and that Jones arranged the donation. These reports document Jones’s role in rally planning and fundraising, but not a White House assignment to lead the march. Organizing the rally and directing a march are distinct responsibilities. The available reporting supports the former while leaving Jones’s claim about White House outreach uncorroborated.

preserved_fields.title: Trump: White House prepares Alex Jones to lead Capitol march on January 6
preserved_fields.description_short: Trump: White House prepares Alex Jones to lead Capitol march on January 6

notes: Needs context: Jones’s claim that the White House contacted him about leading the march is not independently confirmed by the linked CNN report, which documents rally planning and fundraising. Proposed correction: keep the contact attributed to Jones and avoid stating that the White House prepared him unless a direct record or corroborating source identifies the caller.

title: Trump: Biden Admin investigating Trump's influence on scientific decisions
description_short: Trump: Biden Admin investigating Trump's influence on scientific decisions
description_medium: In March 2021, the Biden administration’s Office of Science and Technology Policy announced a task force to review political interference in scientific decisions during the Trump administration. It was intended to examine safeguards for independent federal science and identify past interference, not to punish former officials. The announcement began a review; it did not itself make findings about specific cases.
description_long: In March 2021, the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy announced a task force to examine political interference in scientific decisions during the Trump administration and review policies designed to protect scientific work from political influence. The initiative followed concerns that political officials had affected how federal agencies handled scientific findings. The task force was intended to identify examples and assess institutional safeguards, not to punish former officials for conduct during the prior administration. Its creation therefore began a review process rather than issuing a finding about any particular person or case. The event records an effort by the Biden administration to examine scientific integrity and strengthen protections for evidence-based work in federal agencies. The announcement alone does not establish what the task force later found, which cases it reviewed, or what policy changes followed. Those outcomes require separate documentation from the task force’s work.
organization_tags: Office of Science and Technology Policy

title: Trump: Woman testifies she slept with Matt Gaetz as a minor
description_short: Trump: Woman testifies she slept with Matt Gaetz as a minor
description_medium: A woman told congressional investigators that she had sex with Representative Matt Gaetz when she was 17, according to the timeline. A later House Ethics Committee report separately described allegations involving sex and drugs, which Gaetz denied. The account does not give the hearing date or establish a direct role for Trump in the testimony.
description_long: A woman told congressional investigators that she had sex with Representative Matt Gaetz when she was 17 and still in high school. The timeline says she answered questions over multiple days during a congressional inquiry, but does not identify the session or provide its date. A later House Ethics Committee report described allegations that Gaetz paid women for sex and drugs, including an encounter with a 17-year-old; Gaetz denied wrongdoing. The testimony and the committee’s later findings are separate accounts, and neither should be presented as a criminal conviction. The available record concerns allegations about Gaetz and congressional scrutiny of his conduct. It does not document why the item is prefixed “Trump:” or show that Trump took part in the testimony or investigation. The hearing date and the basis for connecting this event to Trump remain unclear. No criminal verdict is reported in the chronology, and Gaetz denies wrongdoing.

title: Trump: Jay Clayton tapped by Trump to lead SDNY
description_short: Trump: Jay Clayton tapped by Trump to lead SDNY
description_medium: On November 14, 2024, Trump selected former Securities and Exchange Commission chair Jay Clayton to lead the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Southern District of New York. Reuters described the choice as unconventional because Clayton lacked criminal-law experience and noted questions about potential conflicts tied to his corporate work. The selection was not yet a completed appointment.
description_long: Reuters reported on November 14, 2024, that Trump had selected former Securities and Exchange Commission chair Jay Clayton to lead the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Southern District of New York. The office is known for financial-crime and public-corruption cases, making Clayton an unconventional choice, according to the report, because he had no criminal-law experience. His corporate work also raised questions about potential conflicts if companies he had advised became subjects of investigations or prosecutions. At the time, Trump’s selection was a choice for the post, not proof that Clayton had taken office or changed any case. The timeline’s December 5 date conflicts with Reuters’ publication date and the article’s description of the selection, so this account uses November 14. Potential conflicts are questions about future matters and recusal decisions, not evidence that Clayton would favor a client or intervene in a prosecution.
organization_tags: U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Southern District of New York

preserved_fields.title: Trump: Jay Clayton tapped by Trump to lead SDNY
preserved_fields.description_short: Trump: Jay Clayton tapped by Trump to lead SDNY

notes: Reuters’ linked headline and publication date support November 14, 2024 as the selection date; the timeline’s December 5 date was inconsistent. This describes Trump’s selection, not a completed appointment.

title: Indefinite Detention Orders, Family Camps, and Alien Enemies Act Revival
description_short: Indefinite Detention Orders, Family Camps, and Alien Enemies Act Revival
description_medium: Trump administration invoked the Alien Enemies Act to authorize indefinite detention and mass deportation of non-citizens, rerouting hundreds to internment camps at the border and Central America. The administration reissued broad orders to detain and deport immigrants (including refugees and legal residents), citing terrorism and public order, and overruled due process constraints using emergency powers. New legislation, legal maneuvers, and Supreme Court acquiescence expanded legal justification for holding people without charges or trial for as long as determined necessary by the executive branch.
description_long: The Trump administration invoked the Alien Enemies Act in March 2025 to remove Venezuelan men it alleged were members of the Tren de Aragua gang. The American Immigration Council reported that on March 15, officials sent nearly 300 people on three planes to El Salvador, including 238 Venezuelans accused largely on the basis of tattoos and 23 Salvadorans accused of belonging to MS-13. More than 130 of the Venezuelans had pending immigration hearings and had not received removal orders under the usual immigration process, according to the report. The transfers were made under the 1798 wartime statute and an agreement with El Salvador. The report said people on the planes were not told what was happening or given an opportunity to challenge the allegations before transfer. It raises due-process concerns about the use of secret gang accusations. The source documents removals and transfers; it does not establish the title’s claims about family camps or indefinite detention.
subcategory: Indefinite Detention and Due Process Suspension
